findings.fix: "In August 2026, a small Swedish studio, founded by two friends who met in high school, released a game called How to Fish." Line 104: "It was founded by two friends who met in high school."

findings.quote: The game's own content warning on Steam reads, word for word: "cartoon violence towards fish and gambling with fish."
findings.problem: It is a developer-written content descriptor on the Steam page, not a platform content warning. Content Warning is also the name of a different co-op game in this same genre, so this invites confusion. The safe-list string includes '(no real money)', and the quote drops the parenthetical, then the next line says it anyway, so 'word for word' is acceptable only if the parenthetical is delivered in order.
findings.fix: "The developers' own content descriptor on Steam reads, word for word: 'cartoon violence towards fish and gambling with fish.' In parentheses: 'no real money.'" Then keep "Just real fish violence."

findings.quote: We named a whole genre after garbage. And then we bought millions of them.
findings.problem: The dossier says friendslop is a half-joking, half-dismissive label, its origin is disputed, and Castello argued it is not a real genre. 'Bought millions of them' implies millions of games in the genre, which rests on the unverified claim that Peak passed 10M (do_not_say). The only verified number is Alinea's estimate for this one game.
findings.fix: "The internet even invented a name for games like this. Friendslop. Half a joke, half an insult. And this one, by one estimate, sold more than ten million."

findings.quote: Some games just need to get four people in the same place on a Tuesday night.
findings.problem: The Steam page says one to four players, but a patch (1.0.4) raised lobbies to eight, and the dossier says to avoid stating the cap as fixed. The thumbnail has Quest plus three friends, which is four. Narration should not fix the number.
findings.fix: "Some games just need to get a few friends into the same place on a Tuesday night." Keep the thumbnail at four, since it is an illustration, not a claim.

findings.quote: They are slapping each other in the face. Gambling the fish money. Shooting seagulls with a sniper rifle. Losing the boat.
findings.problem: The slap revive, gambling and sniper-and-seagull trick shots are sourced (GamingOnLinux, GameRant). 'Losing the boat' comes only from the unverified reviewer paraphrase ('nobody knows where the boat is') and from the GameRant 'boat's savings' anchor, which is about money. It is repeated as a recurring joke ("the time the boat disappeared", line 92) with no verified source.
findings.fix: Replace the sourced-only items: "Slapping each other in the face. Gambling the fish money. Shooting at seagulls with a sniper rifle. Arguing about where all the money went." Line 92: "They retell the time somebody gambled away the savings."

findings.quote: And that might be the most fitting thing about How to Fish... Their first paid game had not done well. So they made a small game about friends doing something silly together.
findings.problem: The previous game sold below expectations (safe list), but the pivot date and cause are not verified in this pass. 'So they made' presents a causal chain as fact. 'Millions of people answered the same group chat' is rhetoric on top of an estimated number.
findings.fix: "Their previous paid game, Out of Hand: Deluxe, sold well below what they hoped. Then they made a small game about friends doing something silly together. And by one estimate, millions of people answered the group chat."

findings.quote: Everyone in the boat needs their own copy.
findings.problem: The notes say to recheck on the Steam page; the dossier source is the 'each player needs own copy' anchor. The social mechanism rests on it, so if a Friend Pass exists it is false.
findings.fix: Verify on the Steam page at lock. If it holds, keep it; if not, say "Everyone in the boat has to buy in."

findings.quote: Some players say it is short. Some say it is fine alone, just better with friends. Some wonder if it is simply this year's summer hit, and that next year everyone will have moved to the next boat.
findings.problem: The paraphrase of reviews and forum posts is supported for 'short but solid' and 'fine alone' (forum, review), and Player.One raises the 'summer hit' question. These should be attributed as 'reviews' and 'one outlet', and the three lines contradict friendslop being 'only with friends' two paragraphs earlier ('games you only play with friends').
findings.fix: Change the friendslop gloss to "Cheap, chaotic co-op games built for playing with friends." Then: "Reviews say it is short, and fine alone. One outlet asked whether it is just this summer's hit."

findings.quote: Title: Why Did Millions Buy a Fishing Game... to Not Fish?  Thumbnail text: 0 FISH
findings.problem: Title and thumbnail promise a literal contradiction ('to not fish', '0 FISH'). The video delivers a softer one: fishing is the alibi and the goal stays. Players who know the game will see '0 FISH' as false. 'Millions' rests on Alinea's single-source estimate (developer-announced: about a million players). The game name does not appear in the title, which hurts search. The early promise is delivered (the hook line states the ten-million estimate and 'almost nobody is fishing'), but that line is the one that fails fact-checking.
findings.fix: Title: "Why Did So Many People Buy a Fishing Game... and Not Fish?" (or add the game name: "How to Fish: Why Did Millions Buy It... to Not Fish?" only with 'by one estimate' in the description). Thumbnail: change '0 FISH' to 'NOT FISHING' or 'WHY?!'; both variants are already in the file.

findings.quote: Thumbnail: Quest and three friends (Pixie + two new recurring friends) crammed into a tiny rowboat ... a single fish at the edge of the frame
findings.problem: The art is generic and avoids game art, which is correct. The IP note adds no Steam UI, no Discord UI and no Landfall/Peak look. 'Two new recurring friends' are new canon characters that need a spec and credit approval. The group-chat visuals must use our own generic chat bubbles.
findings.fix: Use two generic non-recurring friends in the thumbnail unless the Producer approves new characters. Add to the lock notes: no Steam capsule art or title lettering, no Peak or Lethal Company logos, our own generic chat bubbles.

strengths: Most of the hard facts are verified and attributed: the 1-in-500,000 legendary odds, 'A friend while working hard', the stone-drill prototype, the developer's 'once estimated', and the up-to-100 lobby (Automaton).
The script already avoids 'admitted', the Marketplace-resale motive, 'friends only' and 'no competition'.
The thumbnail promises an original cat, never the game's sprite, which is the right IP call.

findings.quote: Title: Why Do 150,000 People Keep a Cat Watching Them Type?  Hook: "around a hundred and fifty thousand people are playing a game in which nothing happens."  Thumbnail variant: 150,000 OF US
findings.problem: The 147K figure is concurrent Steam players, and the developer estimated about half may be bots (mid-2025, 'we can't know exactly'). The do_not_say list forbids 'hundreds of thousands of people' without qualification. The script itself says later that half the members may be scripts, so the title and hook contradict the body, and the thumbnail variant '150,000 OF US' is worse. SteamCharts moves daily, and a precise '150,000' can be off by publication.
findings.fix: Title: "Why Do So Many Players Keep a Cat Watching Them Type?" Hook: "On an ordinary day, well over a hundred thousand accounts are running a game in which nothing happens." Delete the 150,000 OF US variant. The bot line then pays off the hook instead of contradicting it.

findings.quote: The developer said it was never meant to make money, and reported earning only a few thousand dollars a month.
findings.problem: The revenue figures cover March to June 2025 only (net, about $3,000 a month on average) and are secondhand (WN Hub, Automaton; the Eurogamer original was not opened). The do_not_say list forbids saying the game earns $3K a month today. Stated without a date, the line implies it is current, which is false-sounding for a game at about 150K concurrent.
findings.fix: "In mid-2025, the developer told Eurogamer, as reported by Automaton, that it was making only about three thousand dollars a month, and that it was never meant to make money." Or: "In its first months, it made only a few thousand dollars a month."

findings.quote:
In the multiplayer version, up to a hundred cats can share one lobby. A hundred taskbars. A hundred people somewhere, each alone at a desk, typing their own emails... and for a moment, tapping together.

None of them can see each other's work.
findings.problem: The safe line is only 'up to 100 players' cats can hit the taskbar together in one lobby' (Aug 11, 2025 update, Automaton). It is an update, not a 'version'. 'A hundred people ... each alone at a desk, typing their own emails' invents the lobby members' situation, and by the script's own bot line some of the hundred may be scripts. 'None of them can see each other's work' is unsourced. Automaton also describes teams, so the lobby is not purely ambient.
findings.fix: "Since August 2025, up to a hundred players' cats can share one lobby. A hundred cats, tapping the taskbar at once. Some of them are probably scripts. But the rest are people, each at their own desk." Cut "None of them can see each other's work." or recast it as "Nobody in the lobby can see what the others are typing." after verifying.

findings.quote: So, at its peak, a fan club where maybe half the members were scripts.
findings.problem: The estimate is a mid-2025 'about 50% according to us, but we can't know exactly'. 'At its peak' implies the peak was when half were bots, which the dossier does not say, and 'were scripts' is flatter than 'might be'. The do_not_say list also forbids implying it is half today.
findings.fix: "A fan club where, by the developer's own estimate in 2025, maybe half the members were scripts."

findings.quote: And the game was not even designed as a companion. It began as an experiment with Steam's item market. The very first prototype was a drill digging into a stone.
findings.problem: The safe list: it began around December 2024 as an experiment with Steam's community market, and the first prototype was a drill digging a stone. 'Not even designed as a companion' is the script's inference, and it conflicts with the developer's own 'A friend while working hard' line, which the script has just quoted. The 'strategic success for marketing' note is omitted, which would give a fuller picture.
findings.fix: "And it did not begin as a companion. In late 2024, it was an experiment with Steam's community market. The first prototype was a drill digging into a stone. The cat came later."

findings.quote: And yet people leave it running for hours. Days. Sometimes for most of the time their computer is on.
findings.problem: Supported by a secondary writeup (esports.net: 'days or weeks'; review hours that exceed play time) but not checked. 'Most of the time' is a general claim.
findings.fix: "And yet people leave it running for hours. Sometimes for days."

findings.quote: The developer's own store page describes it in five words: "A friend while working hard."
findings.problem: Verified quote and word count (the Steam page feature list). The phrase 'describes it' slightly oversells a bullet on the feature list. 'The developer' is Irox Games, which is also the publisher.
findings.fix: "The game's own Steam page calls it, in five words, 'A friend while working hard.'"

findings.quote: Title: Why Do 150,000 People Keep a Cat Watching Them Type?  (the game is first named on air at: "Bongo Cat is free.")
findings.problem: The title and the thumbnail do not name the game, and the narration names it only about 45 seconds in. Viewers who searched for 'Bongo Cat' get nothing for 45 seconds. The title's 'watching them' is intentionally ironic (the cat cannot see), and that part is delivered, but the number and 'people' are the problem (C-fact-1). The answer is only fully given in the last minute, which is fine for a contract, as long as the hook shows the cat in the first 5 seconds.
findings.fix: Add the game name to the hook: "A small cat, Bongo Cat, sits at the bottom of your screen." Put the game name in the description and tags, and on screen at 0:00.

findings.quote: Thumbnail: a tiny round cat at the bottom of the screen slapping the taskbar mid-swing ... Our own original cat, never the game's sprite.
findings.problem: The IP direction is correct. The risk is how close 'tiny round cat slapping' gets to the 2018 meme's cat-like blob (art by @StrayRogue and @DitzyFlama, licensing to the Steam game unverified) and to the game's sprite, hats and UI. A taskbar mock-up must also avoid Steam UI and the Marketplace UI.
findings.fix: Give our cat a deliberately distinct silhouette (a different head shape and colours) and no hats from the game. Add to the lock notes: no game footage or GIF, no Billie Eilish cover, and no Steam UI. Use a generic taskbar.

ranking: B: fewest hard problems, since the claims are on the safe list and the main risk is attribution wording ('now', 'two friends', 'almost nobody is fishing') and a literal '0 FISH' thumbnail; all fixable with line edits.

C: one root blocker (150,000 'people', repeated in the title, hook and thumbnail variant, contradicted by the script's own bot line) plus stale-revenue and multiplayer wording; fixable by changing the title and the hook.

A: four on-air blockers (the 'million check daily' claim, 'each one' of the delays quoted, the payoff stating the date as fact, and 'exactly two trailers'), a shaky subreddit inference and a title that is only paid off at the end.

judged.reason: Dossier supports ~949K members, not a million daily checkers. Factual overreach on air; the fix is also tighter.
Line 76 says 'where the delays arrived' and 'Each one' quoted; only the Nov 2025 delay is verified. Fix keeps the farmers line and is more accurate.

Line 116 states the date as fact ('the waiting ends'). Episode lands near launch, so conditional wording is needed. Fix is acceptable but 'If November 19th holds' slightly softens the ending; keep it short and prepare a post-launch variant.
judged.better_fix: "On November 19th, if the date holds, the waiting ends." Keep line 98 as 'On the scheduled day...'.

judged.reason: 'Exactly two trailers' (line 44) can be false by publication and anchors the spine. 'Shown the world two trailers' is nearly as punchy; add RECHECK tag.
Line 64: 'a year before GTA V existed' is false (announced 2011) and the 'which means' inference does not follow. The proposed fix is cleaner.
Line 60 invents a timeline ('By the time GTA VI was delayed again'). Reopen the post and use its words; fix is sound.
'The day after a hearing' is explicitly unconfirmed by KYM. 'Right after' costs nothing.
Bare 'A world record' is checkable against BTS Butter. 'A Guinness record for a videogame reveal' is accurate and loses little punch.

The list is a safe, widely known set; Pope Francis elected March 2013 makes 'a new pope' literally true. Source in lock notes if desired; no line change needed.

Line 86 invents lobby members' situation ('each alone at a desk, typing their own emails') and 'multiplayer version'. Bot line undercuts it. Fix is accurate; keep the warm payoff.
Line 76 'at its peak... were scripts' is flatter than the developer's mid-2025 estimate and misplaces the peak. Attribute to the estimate.

'Not even designed as a companion' is a mild framing consistent with the market-experiment origin; the quoted tagline is marketing copy. Rewrite is a preference, though adding the late-2024 date is harmless.
'Hours. Days.' is supported; 'most of the time their computer is on' is a recognition-gag beat. Trimming it is taste.
Quote and word count are verified; 'describes it' vs 'calls it' is a nitpick.
Game name first appears about 45 seconds in; searchers and viewers get no anchor. Naming the game in the hook is a cheap fix, and also keep it on screen at 0:00.
Thumbnail already specifies an original cat; a distinct silhouette is a lock-notes production note, not an episode defect.

verdict.summary: Most fact findings that touch on-air narration are real: A-fact-1 to A-fact-8, A-pack-1; B-fact-1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 9 and B-pack-1; C-fact-1 to C-fact-4 and C-pack-1. I rejected pure taste, lock-note housekeeping and items the script already handles (A-fact-9 to A-fact-12, A-ip-1, B-fact-3, B-fact-7, B-fact-8, B-ip-1, C-fact-5 to C-fact-7, C-ip-1). Three fixes need tweaks: A-fact-3 (keep the ending shorter), A-fact-8 (say 'Guinness world record') and B-fact-1 (keep 'almost nobody seems to be fishing' as the hook punch). C-fact-1 is the most important fix, since the title, hook and thumbnail variant contradict the script's own bot line.
